I fixed it by rewriting the endpoint to use a single optimized SQL query with joins and indexed filter columns. I also moved the filtering into the database layer and only selected the fields the response actually needed. After that, I re-ran the profiler and load-tested the endpoint again.

The result was that the average search response time dropped from about 2.1 seconds to around 180 ms on the same dataset, and the number of SQL queries per request went from 12–15 down to 1 or 2 depending on the route. That made the final demo much smoother, and it also gave me a good lesson in how to use profiling to find the real bottleneck instead of guessing.

I also removed a couple of unnecessary `SELECT *` calls and only fetched the fields the page actually needed, which reduced the amount of data transferred.

After those changes, I reran the same test dataset and measured the result. The slow page went from about 4.8 seconds to 0.9 seconds on my machine, so it was roughly 5 times faster. I also reduced the number of database queries for that flow from 120 down to 8. I owned the API design and the model integration end to end, and one thing that did not work at first was my original approach to preprocessing and model input.

I fixed it by moving preprocessing into a shared Python module used by both training and the REST endpoint, so the same function handled tokenization, lowercasing, punctuation removal, and input validation in both places. I added unit tests for edge cases like empty strings, repeated spaces, and non-ASCII characters, plus an integration test that sent sample requests through the API and checked the stored SQL records and returned predictions. After that, the model behavior became consistent between training and production-like requests, and the validation accuracy on my test set improved from about 71% to 84%.

What I learned was that in ML-related software, the model is only one part of the system. If the preprocessing, API, and data storage are not aligned, the whole result can look broken even when the model itself is fine. Since then, I always try to make the data flow explicit, share code where it makes sense, and write tests around the boundaries between components.

On the training set, the accuracy was around 92%, so I thought we were in good shape. But when I tested it on a held-out validation set, performance dropped to about 68%, and the model was especially bad at the smaller classes. That was the first sign that something in the design was off, not just the model itself.

I dug into the error cases and realized two things. First, I had been tuning the model while looking too much at the training results, which made me overestimate how well it generalized. Second, our validation split was not representative enough because the classes were imbalanced. I changed the workflow so we used a proper train/validation split with stratification, and I compared several options using the validation set instead of the training score. I also added n-grams to the TF-IDF features and set `class_weight='balanced'` in logistic regression. That helped the model pay more attention to the smaller labels.

After those changes, validation accuracy improved from 68% to 81%, and macro F1 went up by about 14 points. More importantly, the model stopped missing the minority categories as often, which made the final demo much more convincing. The main thing I learned was that a design decision can look fine on paper, but if you don’t validate it properly, you can end up optimizing for the wrong thing. Since then, I’ve been much more careful about using a validation set early and checking class balance before trusting any metric.
